sections.body: Reading the Market's Language is the part of The AI Economist that treats financial text as data. Artificial intelligence here parses earnings call transcripts, supply chain updates, retail investor posts, news wires, and regulatory filings. It scores tone, extracts entities, links events to instruments, and flags changes in language that may matter to markets. In practice, this means models that classify sentences, summarize long documents, and compare a company's words across quarters. The work is not about a single magic model, it is about pipelines that clean text, tag it, and feed signals into research. The site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, which gives these text signals a market baseline to compare against.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are mature. Tone scoring, named entity recognition, and document summarization work well enough to be used in research workflows. What is not solved is causality. A negative tone on a call does not tell you why, and a supply chain mention does not tell you whether a delay will hit revenue. Models can miss sarcasm, hedging, and legal boilerplate, and they can overfit to past market reactions. Regulatory filings are especially hard because they are written to be precise and defensive, not to be clear. The honest limit is that these tools produce signals, not answers, and they need human review before anyone treats them as meaningful.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section divide the text sources by where the language comes from. Earnings Call Tone looks at management language, guidance shifts, and analyst questions. Supply Chain Disruption in Text follows supplier updates, shipping notices, and logistics language for early signs of stress. Retail Investor Sentiment covers forums, social posts, and crowd mood, which is noisy but fast. Event-Driven Trading connects news and announcements to price moves around specific events. Reading Regulatory Filings handles the dense legal and compliance text, and the site's 355 merger and acquisition filings, 148 active AI lawsuits, and 219 compliance and regulation pages give that page a concrete corpus to work from. A reader would go to each page for a different text source, then combine them to see how language and markets interact.
